source_text: πρὸς μείζονα οὐ πρεσβεύει, ἀλλ' ὡς αὐτοκράτωρ συγχωρεῖ. 26.32 Ματθαῖος δέ, συνεισφέρων καὶ αὐτὸς ταῖς περὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς υἱοῦ θεολογίαις, ἔφη· «οὐδεὶς γινώσκει τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις ἐπιγινώσκει, εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ». 26.33 Πῶς τοίνυν οὗτοι φιλονεικοῦσιν ὡς εἰδότες τὸν μὲν πατέρα ἀσύγκριτον, τὸν δὲ υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἀνόμοιον αὐτῷ, τὴν δὲ οὐσίαν ἀγεννησίαν· οὐδὲν ἐξαίρετον τῇ γνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς θεοῦ καταλιμπάνοντες 26.34 οὐδὲ λογιζόμενοι, ὅτιπερ οὐδὲν ἑτεροφυὲς ἴσην τῷ ἑτεροουσίῳ κέκτηται γνῶσιν; 26.35 Παῦλος δὲ ὁμοίως γράφει Τιμοθέῳ μὲν ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ἐπιστολῇ· «προστάσσω σοὶ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζωοποιοῦντος τὰ πάντα καὶ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ μαρτυρήσαντος ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν, φυλάξαι τὴν παραγγελίαν ἄσπιλον, ἀνεπίληπτον ἕως τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἣν καιροῖς ἰδίοις δείξει ὁ μακάριος καὶ μόνος δυνατὸς καὶ βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων, ὁ μόνος ἔχων ἀθανασίαν καὶ φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον, ὃν οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων εἶδεν οὔτε ἰδεῖν δύναται, ᾧ τιμὴ καὶ δόξα αἰώνιος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν». 26.36 αἱρετικοῖς μὲν γὰρ δέδοκται τῷ πατρὶ μόνῳ διδόναι τό· «ὁ μόνος δυνατὸς καὶ βασιλεὺς βασιλευόντων» καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. 26.37 ὥσπερ δὲ περὶ ἀμφοῖν τῶν ἀειμνήστων ὑποστάσεων εἶπεν· «προστάσσω σοὶ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ», οὕτως ἐπ' ἀμφοῖν αὐτῶν ὡς κατὰ ἑνὸς τῇ θεότητι καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς ὕμνησεν. 26.38 οὐ γὰρ ὡς οὗτοι ἠγνόησεν αὐτὸς τό· «πάντα ὅσα ἔχει ὁ πατὴρ ἐμά ἐστιν», καὶ τό· «ἵνα πάντες τιμῶσι τὸν υἱὸν καθὼς τιμῶσι τὸν πατέρα», καὶ τό· «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἀληθινὸς θεὸς καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνιος», καί· «οὗτος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν. οὐ λογισθήσεται ἕτερος πρὸς αὐτόν», καί· «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός». 26.39 ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀποτείνεται μᾶλλον τὰ ἐκκείμενα πρὸς τὸν υἱόν. ἔχει γάρ· «παραφυλάξαι τὴν παραγγελίαν ἕως τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χρι στοῦ, ἣν καιροῖς ἰδίοις δείξει ὁ μακάριος καὶ μόνος δυνατός». 26.40 δῆλον δ' ὅτι ὁ υἱὸς δείξει τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφάνειαν τὸ δεύτερον ἐλευσόμενος. ἐπιτήρει οὖν ὅτι καὶ δόξαν τὴν πρώτην αὐτῷ ἀπονέμει. 26.41 Ῥωμαίοις δέ· «τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασιν νοούμενα καθο ρᾶται, ἥ τε ἀίδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης». 26.42 καὶ ταυτὶ δὲ διὰ τὴν ἰσοτιμίαν πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ οὐ ῥέπει πρὸς ποίημα. 26.43 οὐ γὰρ ἐν τῷ γεννητὸν νοεῖσθαι τὸν δημιουργὸν ἡ ἀιδιότης καὶ θειότης αὐτοῦ οὐ γνωρίζεται, τουτέστιν ἡ ἀεὶ καὶ κατὰ ταὐτὰ ἔχουσα θεότης. 26.44 Φιλιππησίοις δέ· «ὃς ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, ἀλλ' ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν μορφὴν δούλου λαβών». 26.45 τί τῆς ἰσότητος ταύτης εὑρίσκεται ἄνισον; οὐχ ἥρπασε γάρ, φησίν, οὐκ ἔλαβε τὸ ἴσον εἶναι τῇ φύσει τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί. καὶ δὴ ὁ μὴ ὑπ' ἄλλου κενωθείς, ἑαυτὸν δὲ κενώσας, αὐθέντην δεσπότην ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀίδιον ἑαυτὸν ἐπέδειξεν. 26.46 εἰ γὰρ ἐγένετο ἐν δούλου μορφῇ, ἀναμφίλογον ὡς οὐ διετέλει, πρὶν 26.46 ἢ τοῦτο γένηται, ἐν ποιήμασιν, ἀλλ' ἐν ἐλευθέρᾳ τῇ πατρικῇ φύσει ἦν. ἐπειδὴ μὴ δυνατὸν ἦν ὀφθῆναι, συγκατέβη ἀτρέπτως ἀφαντασιάστως ἕως οἰκέτου μορφῆς. 26.47 καὶ τὰ τοῦ οἰκέτου ἀπώσατο ἄχθη καὶ ζωῆς φαιδροτέρας δέδωκεν ἀρχήν· ὅθεν 28 καὶ ὅστις ἀνάρχως ἦν ἐπεγνώσθη. 26.48 Καὶ τὰ ἄλλα δὲ τὰ ἐπισταλέντα τοῖς αὐτοῖς Φιλιππησίοις, ὅτι ἤδη πως τὸν υἱὸν προὔχοντά τε καὶ ὑπερβάλλοντα σὺν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ πατρὶ ὅσον πρὸς ἀσυνέτους ἀποφαίνει, ἤδη μοι λέλεκται πρόσθεν ἐν κεφαλαίῳ ζʹ. 26.49 κωλύει δὲ οὐδέν, καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχαίας τοῦτο συστῆσαι γραφῆς· δεῖ γὰρ μὴ παρέργως κεχρῆσθαι τῇ θεολογίᾳ. 26.50 Λέγει οὖν παρὰ τῷ Ἠσαΐᾳ ὁ θεός· «τὰς νουμηνίας ὑμῶν καὶ τὰ σάββατα καὶ τὰς ἑορτὰς ὑμῶν μισεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου. ἐγενήθητέ μοι εἰς πλησμονήν· οὐκέτι ἀνήσω τὰς ἁμαρτίας ὑμῶν. κἂν πληρώ σητε τὴν δέησιν, οὐκ εἰσακούσομαι ὑμῶν· αἱ γὰρ χεῖρες ὑμῶν αἵματος πλή ρεις. λούσασθε, καθαροὶ γένεσθε, ἀφέλετε τὰς ἁμαρτίας ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῶν ψυχῶν ὑμῶν». 26.51 ὁρᾷς τοίνυν, ὅτι καὶ φθάνει φιλανθρωπία τὴν ἀπειλήν, ὅσον οὐδέπω διαλλαττόμενος καὶ μηνιεῖν μακρά, μᾶλλον δὲ μηνιεῖν ὅλως οὐκ εἰδώς. 26.52 καὶ μισεῖ τὰς ἑορτὰς αὐτῶν, ὅ ἐστι τὴν θρησκείαν, ὡς τῆς τελεωτάτης θεογνωσίας ἀπολειπομένην· παρακελεύεται δὲ βαπτισθῆναι ὥστε δέξασθαι τὴν πίστιν πρὸς τὸν περὶ τοῦ βαπτίσματος δεσποτικὸν ὅρον. 26.53 ἐπιστώσατο δὲ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ ὁ Παῦλος ἐπὶ λέξεως ἀνακεκραγώς, μὴ
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: ... that, as if] he does not act as envoy to a greater one, but as absolute ruler forgives. 26.32 And Matthew, himself too contributing to the theologies about the only-begotten Son, said: 'no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone fully know the Son except the Father'. 26.33 How then do these men contend as knowing the Father to be incomparable, and his Son unlike him, and the essence unbegottenness, leaving nothing set apart for the knowledge of God the Father and of the only-begotten God, 26.34 nor reckoning that nothing of another nature has acquired knowledge equal to the one of another essence? 26.35 And Paul likewise writes, to Timothy in the first letter: 'I command you before God who gives life to all things and Jesus Christ who bore witness under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, to keep the commandment spotless, irreproachable until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only mighty one will show, both King of those reigning and Lord of those ruling, the one alone having immortality and dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no one of men saw nor can see, to whom be honor and eternal glory to the ages of the ages. Amen'. 26.36 For it has seemed good to heretics to give to the Father alone the 'the only mighty one and King of those reigning' and the following. 26.37 But just as about both the ever-remembered hypostases he said: 'I command you before God and Christ Jesus', so about both of them, as about one in Godhead, he hymned the following too. 26.38 For he himself was not ignorant, as these are, of the 'all things whatever the Father has are mine', and the 'that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father', and the 'this is the true God and eternal life', and 'this is our God; another will not be reckoned beside him', and 'this is my Son, the beloved'. 26.39 But rather the things set out are stretched toward the Son. For it has: 'to guard the commandment until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only mighty one will show'. 26.40 And it is clear that the Son will show his own appearing, coming the second time. Observe then that he assigns to him the first glory too. 26.41 And to the Romans: 'for his invisible things from the creation of the world are seen, being understood by the things made, both his eternal power and divinity'. 26.42 And these things too, on account of the equal honor of Father and Son, do not tilt toward a thing made. 26.43 For not in the Creator's being thought begotten is his eternity and divinity not made known, that is, the Godhead that is always and according to the same things. 26.44 And to the Philippians: 'who, being in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God a seizing, but emptied himself, having taken the form of a slave'. 26.45 What of this equality is found unequal? For he did not seize, he says; he did not take the being equal by nature to God and Father. And indeed the one not emptied by another but having emptied himself showed himself at once master in his own right and eternal. 26.46 For if he came to be in a slave's form, it is indisputable that he did not continue, before [this repeated number 26.46 is debris] this came to be, among things made, but he was in the free paternal nature. Since it was not possible to be seen, he came down together without turning, without illusion, as far as a household servant's form. 26.47 And he thrust away the burdens of the household servant and gave a beginning of a brighter life; whence [page number 28: skipped] he who was without beginning also was recognized. 26.48 And the other things sent to the same Philippians, that already somehow he declares the Son excelling and surpassing together with his own Father, as far as concerns the unintelligent, have already been spoken by me before in chapter seven. 26.49 And nothing prevents establishing this from the ancient Scripture too; for one must not use theology as a by-work. 26.50 So God says in Isaiah: 'your new moons and the sabbaths and your feasts my soul hates. You have become to me for a surfeit; I will no longer let go your sins. Even if you fill up the prayer, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood. pass_b_english: … does not plead with one greater, but forgives as sovereign.

Matthew too, adding his own share to what is taught of the only-begotten Son as God, said: “No one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father” (Matthew 11:27). How then do these men quarrel as though they knew the Father to be incomparable, his Son to be unlike him, and his essence to be unbegottenness? They leave nothing as the special preserve of the knowledge that belongs to God the Father and the only-begotten God, and they do not reckon that nothing of a different nature has a knowledge equal to that of a being whose essence is other than its own.

Paul likewise writes to Timothy in the first letter: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who bore witness to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment spotless and blameless until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will show, the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one among men has seen or can see; to whom be honor and eternal glory to the ages of ages. Amen” (1 Timothy 6:13–16). The heretics have resolved to give to the Father alone the words “the only Mighty One and King of those who reign” and what follows. But just as Paul spoke of both the ever-remembered hypostases, “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus,” so he sang the praises that follow of both of them, as of one in Godhead. For he was not ignorant, as these men are, of “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15), and “that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23), and “This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20), and “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him” (Baruch 3:35), and “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17).

Rather, the words set out here point more toward the Son. For the text runs: “to keep the commandment until the appearing of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only Mighty One will show” (1 Timothy 6:14–15). And it is plain that the Son will show his own appearing when he comes the second time. Observe, then, that Paul assigns to him the first glory too.

And to the Romans: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, both his eternal power and divinity” (Romans 1:20). These words too, because Father and Son are equal in honor, do not tilt toward a thing made. For the Creator’s being understood as begotten does not keep his eternity and divinity from being known, that is, his Godhead, which is always and in the same way. And to the Philippians: “Who, being in the form of God, did not count being equal to God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave” (Philippians 2:6–7).

What in this equality is found unequal? “He did not seize it,” Paul says; he did not take to himself his being equal by nature to God the Father. And indeed he who was emptied by no one else, but emptied himself, showed himself to be at once Master in his own right and eternal. For if he came to be in the form of a slave, it is beyond dispute that before this happened he did not dwell among things made, but was in the free nature of the Father. Since he could not be seen, he came down, without change and not in mere appearance, as far as the form of a household slave. He thrust off the slave’s burdens and gave the beginning of a brighter life; and so he who was without beginning came to be known.

As for the other things written to these same Philippians, in which Paul already shows in some way, as far as the unintelligent need it, that the Son is pre-eminent and supreme together with his own Father, I have already spoken of them above, in the seventh chapter. But nothing prevents our establishing this from the ancient Scripture as well, for theology must not be handled in passing. So God says in Isaiah: “Your new moons and sabbaths and your feasts my soul hates. You have become a surfeit to me; I will no longer let your sins go. Even if you make your prayer full, I will not hear you, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, become clean, take away your sins from your souls” (Isaiah 1:13–16).

You see, then, that his love for mankind runs ahead even of his threat: he is all but reconciled already, and does not know how to keep his anger long, or rather how to be angry at all. He hates their feasts, that is, their worship, because it falls short of the most perfect knowledge of God; and he bids them be baptized, so as to receive the faith according to the Master’s ordinance for baptism. choices.issue: Old draft garbled, with reversed and invented claims and missing references
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English made 26.34 say one 'possesses knowledge equal to the homoousion'; split Romans 1:20 into a broken quotation ('for his invisible things from...') and a garbled clause with no reference; reversed the double negative of 26.43 ('is not to be understood in the Begotten'); attached 'in creatures' to the Father's nature and gave ἀφαντασιάστως as 'invisibly' (26.46); made 26.48 say Paul 'holds the Son before and above his own Father as far as he decides toward the irrational'; 26.40 'it allows that he also grant him'; 26.49 'use theology as a pastime'; 26.51 'even philanthropy reaches the threat … not yet exchanging [them]'; 26.52 'he is exhorted to be baptized'. References: Isaiah 1:15-16 widened to 1:13-16 (new moons and sabbaths are 1:13); Philippians 2:6 widened to 2:6-7; Romans 1:20 and 1 Timothy 6:14-15 added; four abbreviated references written out.

choices.why: A second printing of the edition number and a page number in the copy-text; skipped.

choices.english: … does not plead with one greater
choices.why: The sentence begins in the previous section ('that, as it were, …'); only the words held here are translated, opening with an ellipsis.

choices.term: οὐδὲν ἐξαίρετον τῇ γνώσει τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς θεοῦ καταλιμπάνοντες
choices.english: They leave nothing as the special preserve of the knowledge that belongs to God the Father and the only-begotten God
choices.why: Read against Matthew 11:27: the Father and the Son alone know each other, and the opponents claim that knowledge for themselves. See problems.
The Eunomian formula that the Father's essence is unbegottenness itself; 'unbegotten' (old draft) blurs it.

choices.term: οὐδὲν ἑτεροφυὲς ἴσην τῷ ἑτεροουσίῳ κέκτηται γνῶσιν
choices.english: nothing of a different nature has a knowledge equal to that of a being whose essence is other than its own
choices.why: A thing cannot know as an equal what differs from it in essence; so the mutual knowledge of Father and Son shows one essence. See problems.

choices.english: the blessed and only Mighty One
choices.why: Didymus' text has δυνατός for the Bible's δυνάστης; translated as he gives it.
ἀείμνηστος is 'of everlasting memory', a term of reverence; 'eternal' (old draft) is a different word.
Kept literal: the glory of the doxology, given to the Son as well as the Father.

choices.english: do not tilt toward a thing made
choices.why: The 'eternal power' of Romans 1:20 is not to be bent into meaning something created.

choices.term: οὐ γὰρ … ἡ ἀιδιότης καὶ θειότης αὐτοῦ οὐ γνωρίζεται
choices.english: the Creator’s being understood as begotten does not keep his eternity and divinity from being known
choices.why: The two negatives cancel: being begotten does not hide the Son's eternity.

choices.term: οὐχ ἥρπασε γάρ, φησίν, οὐκ ἔλαβε
choices.english: “He did not seize it,” Paul says; he did not take to himself
choices.why: Didymus restates ἁρπαγμός: the equality was his, not a thing grasped or received.

choices.english: without change and not in mere appearance
choices.why: Against both a change in the Word and a docetic, illusory incarnation.

choices.english: as far as the unintelligent need it
choices.why: Didymus' hedge: Paul's words in Philippians are already enough to answer the slow-witted.
Didymus' own cross-reference within the work, kept in words.

choices.english: he is all but reconciled already
choices.why: ὅσον οὐδέπω, 'all but, on the point of'.

choices.term: ἐπὶ λέξεως ἀνακεκραγώς, μὴ (end of section)
choices.english: crying aloud in so many words that he does not …
choices.why: The sentence continues in the next section (μὴ / ἔχειν ἑαυτοῦ μείζονα τὸν υἱόν); only the negative held here is translated, ending with an ellipsis, so it joins u08-open's '… have anyone greater than himself: the Son'.
